items.content_html:
In addition to the resources already mentioned, there’s lots of general & design-level warp mitigation solutions and information in this post:

Large Prints: Say Goodbye to Warping! Community Contributions
[翘边_首图_en] How often does this situation happen to you? The printer has printed half of the model. The model’s bottom lifts off the print bed - warping. We need to trash the whole model. Large prints tend to warp, like furniture parts. When we make 3D-printed tools and add more wall layers to make them stronger, they sometimes warp. You can see how warping looks and where it occurs in the image below. [image] In our first Bambu Lab flagstore, you can see and experience the massive CyberBr…

Personally, if a brim or mouse ears aren’t enough to reliably hold the print down, it’s usually back to the design for me. Even with glue as adhesive (eg. on Engineering plate), a bad warp may lift the plate instead (which can be hard to notice). And I don’t like glue anyway.

Cheers,
-Max

items.title: [andi@undisclosed.example.com andi] Still Alive revived
items.content_html:
Still Alive revived

Back in 2008, I blogged about a little homebrew game for the Nintendo DS named StillAliveDS and how much I liked the puzzle platformer.

StillAliveDS is a puzzle game inspired by Portal: The Flash Version, which is a 2D remake of Portal, developed by Valve Corporation.

Portal consists primarily of a series of puzzles that must be solved by teleporting the character and other simple objects using a Portal Gun. The unusual physics allowed by the Portal Gun are the emphasis of Portal.

A few weeks ago, I used my website's random button and landed on exactly that post. I wondered whatever became of the game. To my surprise, I learned that its developer, “t4ils,” had made a web version and released it under the AGPL.

Unfortunately, the website was no longer available, but the Wayback Machine still had parts of it. There was enough to recover all the client-side code.

It still worked in modern browsers, but it used an ancient version of jQuery, and the tiny DS-resolution graphics weren't great on modern systems.

So I spent quite some time “reviving” the game with the help of Claude. I wanted to keep the gameplay, look, and feel as close to the original as possible while thoroughly modernizing the game.

To nobody's surprise, Claude was able to make the game run again in no time. Refactoring the code and graphics into a modern architecture, on the other hand, took a lot of babysitting and reviewing. The current architecture is the result of many, many iterations.

Tiles and background graphics had to be redrawn from scratch while staying close to the original. Though I made the creative decision to drop a few “jokes” from the background images that I felt were a bit out of date – I don't think anyone misses jokes about Michael Jackson's looks in 2026.

Since the licensing of the original audio was a bit unclear, I decided to replace the sound effects and also extend them to cover more actions. Finding the right effects took quite a while – Claude helped me by building a “sound lab” where I could test and compare sound effects from different free sources until I found what I needed.

Even though the game now uses a modern ES module structure and web components for the UI, I decided not to use a bundler. Instead, it relies on modern browsers' module-loading support. A custom loader loads all assets into RAM once. This way, there are no external dependencies (neither libraries nor build tools), and the game can be restored from the Wayback Machine, just like the original could.

The game can be played right in your browser: Still Alive revived.

Currently, only mouse and keyboard are supported. If I feel like it, I might add controller support someday. I don't know if or how it could ever be made to support touch controls.

items.title: [Dreaming3D Inc - News] Bambu Lab at Costco
items.content_html:
&&&

Bambu Lab at Costco · A1 Combo bundle · San Diego · November 21, 2026

Bambu Lab at Costco: What the $419.99 A1 Combo Bundle Gets You, and Who Fixes It When It Jams

Costco’s website sells a Bambu Lab A1 Combo bundle. We priced it against Bambu’s own store, read both return policies and Bambu’s warranty fine print, and mapped out who fixes what when it jams.

A 3D printer for sale a few clicks from the bulk paper towels still feels a little strange, but here we are. Costco’s site lists a Bambu Lab A1 Combo bundle, item 2066547, at $419.99: the A1 printer, its AMS lite four-spool feeder, four spools of Bambu’s PLA Basic, and two spare hotends. When we checked on November 21, 2026, it showed out of stock for delivery to a San Diego ZIP code and out of stock in-warehouse at a San Diego location.

So is it a deal? That turns on two things the listing doesn’t spell out: how much filament is on those four spools, and whether Bambu treats a Costco receipt like one from its own store. We repair Bambu printers across San Diego County, so we also cover the part nobody prices in: who fixes it when it jams.

$419.99Costco’s online price for the bundle, item 2066547, on Nov 21.
$359.00Bambu’s US store price for the A1 Combo alone the same day ($399.00 regular).
$9.25What each of the four spools has to be worth for the bundle to beat Bambu’s sale (our arithmetic).
1 yearThe warranty Costco’s listing states. Bambu’s 2-year US term is written for its own store’s buyers.

The short version

  • What you get: an A1 Combo (the A1 plus the AMS lite feeder), four PLA Basic spools, a 0.4 mm hardened steel hotend and a 0.2 mm stainless hotend. Bambu’s own A1 Combo box has 20 g of sample filament and the stock 0.4 mm hotend.
  • Price: at Bambu’s sale price, the printer and the same two hotends cost $382.98. The bundle costs $37.01 more, so the four spools have to be worth $9.25 each. Full 1 kg spools would be; the listing doesn’t give a weight (our arithmetic).
  • Only want the printer? Bambu’s store was $60.99 cheaper on Nov 21. At Bambu’s regular $399.00, the bundle wins before you count the spools.
  • Returns: Costco’s guarantee is the bundle’s strongest card. 3D printers aren’t on Costco’s 90-day electronics list, but the policy says limitations apply, so ask at the membership counter and keep the box.
  • Warranty: plan on 1 year from Bambu, not 2, and ask Bambu to confirm coverage on your serial number with the Costco receipt before anything breaks. Costco wasn’t on Bambu’s US reseller list when we checked.
  • Repairs: inside the warranty, open a Bambu ticket first. Hotends, nozzles, plates and PTFE tubes aren’t covered by anyone’s warranty, and that’s where we come in, along with setup ($159.99 for printers bought elsewhere), out-of-warranty repair and video help.

Five things the listing and the deal threads get wrong

The A1 isn’t enclosed.
Costco’s spec table lists the A1’s features as “Enclosured.” It’s an open-frame printer with a bed that slides front to back, and Bambu’s own FAQ says it doesn’t recommend enclosing the A1. Bambu lists PLA, PETG, TPU and PVA as the A1’s ideal filaments, and the moving bed needs clearance in front and behind.
Its top speed is 500 mm/s, not 550.
The listing gives 550 mm/s. Bambu’s spec page lists a 500 mm/s maximum toolhead speed and 10,000 mm/s² acceleration. Either way, that’s a ceiling, not the speed a typical print runs at.
Bambu’s 2-year US warranty is written for its own store.
Bambu moved US and Canada printers to two years in August. Its policy page, updated Sept 22, 2026, says that extension applies to products bought through Bambu Store US and Bambu Store CA. Costco’s listing says 1 year. Bambu also says only receipts from Bambu or “distributors authorized by Bambu Lab” count for warranty, and Costco wasn’t among the 48 US and Canada sellers on Bambu’s authorized reseller list on Nov 21. Ask Bambu to confirm your coverage in writing.
The $50 gift card is gone, and so is $50.
A July deal post listed the bundle at $469.99 with a $50 Bambu.com gift card. On Nov 21, Costco’s page showed $419.99 and no gift card in the box list. It’s the same math either way: $469.99 minus $50 of store credit is $419.99.
Skip the support email printed on the listing.
The address on Costco’s page has a typo in the domain. Bambu says warranty cases go through its support page, so start there.

What’s in the Costco box, and what’s in Bambu’s

Costco’s bundle is built on the same A1 Combo Bambu sells: the A1, a bed-slinger with a 256 mm cube of build space, plus the AMS lite, the open four-spool feeder that switches colors for you. The difference is what comes with it.

Item Costco bundle Bambu US store A1 Combo
Printer and feeder A1 and AMS lite A1 and AMS lite
Filament Four PLA Basic spools; the listing doesn’t give a weight 20 g of sample filament, random color
Hotends The A1’s pre-installed 0.4 mm stainless hotend, plus spare 0.4 mm hardened steel and 0.2 mm stainless hotends The pre-installed 0.4 mm stainless hotend
Gift card Listed in July; not in the box list on Nov 21 None
Price on Nov 21 $419.99 $359.00 sale, $399.00 regular
Shipping UPS Ground included Free in the 48 contiguous states

The spare hotends are the useful part. Bambu’s hotend page says its carbon-fiber PLA and PETG run with a low risk of clogging in a 0.4 mm hardened steel nozzle, and warns that filament filled with carbon fiber, glass fiber or metal is prone to clog a 0.2 mm nozzle. So the 0.2 mm hotend is for fine detail in plain filament, and the hardened one is for Bambu’s carbon-fiber PLA and PETG. When a swap is the fix, our A1 hotend guide walks through it.

The price math, two ways

Prices move every few days in late November, so treat these as a snapshot from Nov 21. All of it is our arithmetic on prices we read that day.

Line Price Where it comes from
Costco bundle $419.99 costco.com, item 2066547
A1 Combo at Bambu’s US store $359.00 Sale price; $399.00 regular
0.4 mm hardened steel A1 hotend $11.99 Bambu US store
0.2 mm stainless A1 hotend $11.99 Bambu US store
Printer plus the same two hotends $382.98 Our arithmetic
Left for the four spools $37.01 ($9.25 each) Our arithmetic
PLA Basic 1 kg refill at Bambu $14.99 list; $9.74 at 10+ rolls Bambu US store; refills come without a spool

Read it two ways. If you only want the printer, Bambu’s store was $60.99 cheaper on Nov 21, and Bambu’s 30-day return window and 2-year US warranty come with a store purchase. If you’d buy filament and a hardened steel hotend anyway, the bundle comes out ahead as long as each spool is worth more than $9.25. Four full 1 kg rolls would be worth $59.96 at Bambu’s refill list price and $38.96 at its 10-roll price, both above the $37.01 gap (our arithmetic).

Against Bambu’s regular $399.00, the bundle is already $2.99 cheaper before you count the spools. The catch is the weight: Costco’s page says four PLA Basic filaments and stops there. If they turn out to be small sample spools, the sale price at Bambu wins. The label on each spool will tell you; a kitchen scale will too.

Costco isn’t the only shelf with an A1 on it. Bambu’s reseller list includes Best Buy and Micro Center, and our budget multicolor roundup compares the A1 Combo with its rivals under $500. If multicolor is the point, read our purge waste guide too: every color change burns some filament, and it adds up.

Returns: Costco’s strongest card

Costco’s satisfaction guarantee promises a refund on merchandise you’re not happy with, with a short list of exceptions and no general time limit written into it. The exception that matters here is electronics, which get a 90-day window: televisions, projectors, major appliances, computers, touchscreen tablets, smart wearables, cameras, drones, camcorders, MP3 players and cell phones. 3D printers aren’t on that list.

The policy also says “Limitations apply” and points members to the membership counter. We read it as the general guarantee covering a printer, and we wouldn’t bet a purchase on that reading. We’re not lawyers. Ask at the counter before day 90 and keep the box. We read the policy the same way for the Creality K2 bundle Costco sells.

Online orders can go back to any Costco warehouse, and Costco says there are more than 800 of them, or you can start the return on costco.com. Bambu’s own return window is 30 days from delivery for its store’s buyers, and its policy says products bought from a reseller follow the reseller’s return and replacement rules. For a Costco unit, the return counter is the first stop for anything wrong out of the box.

What the counter can’t do is fix it. Costco’s Technical and Warranty Services offers free support for TVs, computers, tablets, cameras, appliances, home theater gear and printers, and nothing on that page mentions 3D printers. Call and ask, but expect to troubleshoot an A1 with Bambu’s support or with a local shop.

Warranty: what Bambu covers, and for how long

Bambu’s policy page gives a warranty term for every listed part of the A1 and the AMS lite. We drew it as a rack in the figure above: 34 parts at the full term, 4 at three months, and 14 with no warranty at all. That’s our count of the entries on Bambu’s two lists, so a part listed on both counts twice; filament and Maker’s Supply items are left out.

Part group Examples from Bambu’s list Bambu’s term First call
Main printer parts Mainboard, AC and TH boards, motors, belts, heatbed unit, touch screen, camera, fans 24 months* Bambu ticket
AMS lite main parts Mainboard, housing, feeder motor, filament hub, stand 24 months* Bambu ticket
Three-month parts Extruder unit (not its gears or sensor), AMS lite feeder unit, rotary spool holder, microSD card 3 months Bambu ticket, then us
No warranty Hotend with nozzle, heater, thermistor and sock; extruder gears; build plates; PTFE tubes; filament cutter; nozzle wiper; AMS lite funnels and spool claws None You, or us

*24 months is the term on Bambu’s US page, and its policy ties that term to Bambu Store US purchases. Costco’s listing says 1 year.

No warranty doesn’t mean no help. Bambu says it will replace consumables that fail from a manufacturing defect while the printer itself is in warranty, at its discretion. Wear is on you.

Bambu’s claim rules matter if you want a local repair. It wants a ticket through its support page first, with the receipt and photos, video or logs of the problem. It asks owners not to repair damage themselves without its guidance, and it says the warranty becomes invalid if an unauthorized service center works on the printer without its approval. That’s why, inside the warranty, we’ll ask you to open the ticket before we open the printer. If Bambu sends a part, ask on the ticket whether a local tech can install it, and we’ll do it once they say yes. Our support-ticket guide covers what to do when a ticket stalls.

Two more notes. Bambu says its terms don’t take away rights you have under state law, and California has its own warranty rules; we’re not lawyers. And if you’ve read about the A1’s 2024 recall over its heatbed cable, Bambu says A1 printers sold after January 30, 2024 already have the fixes, and Costco’s listing describes the reinforced cable.

What breaks on an A1 Combo, and who fixes it

Here’s how common A1 Combo problems line up with Bambu’s parts list, and what the parts cost on Bambu’s US store.

Problem Usual suspects Part and price Who handles it
Clog, thin or gappy lines Heat creep, damp or dusty filament, filled filament in the 0.2 mm nozzle A1 hotend: $9.99 (0.4 mm stainless) or $11.99 (0.4 mm hardened or 0.2 mm stainless) You can swap a hotend; there’s no warranty on hotends. We clear clogs on visits.
A blob of plastic around the hotend A print that lets go of the plate while the nozzle keeps extruding Heating assembly $19.99, silicone sock $2.99 (Bambu US store, Oct 22) Us, once it’s past the sock
AMS lite won’t feed or keeps retrying A tangled or cracked spool, a worn PTFE tube, the feeder unit PTFE tubes: no warranty. Feeder unit: 3 months Bambu in the first 3 months, then us
Prints won’t stick Fingerprints or wear on the plate, damp filament Build plates: no warranty You, with our plate guide
Layer shifts, grinding, a dead screen or board Belts, motors, the mainboard, the heatbed unit 24-month parts on Bambu’s list Bambu ticket first; us after the warranty

The details live in our guides: clearing a clogged Bambu, the blob of death, AMS feed problems, build plates that hold and when to swap an A1 hotend.

Your first week with a Costco A1 Combo

Do these in order. The first three cost nothing and save the most trouble later.

1Keep the box and every bit of foam

Costco’s return counter and Bambu’s warranty shipping both go easier with the original packaging.

Bambu’s policy says original packaging gives the best protection in transit, and that poor packing can mean extra repair charges or denied coverage for shipping damage. Don’t flatten anything until you know the printer is a keeper.

2Photograph the serial number and save the Costco order

Bambu asks for the receipt and evidence with every claim, so get both on file on day one.

Photograph the serial label and the box label, and save the costco.com order email as a PDF. If something fails in month eleven, you won’t be hunting for them.

3Ask Bambu to confirm your warranty

Open a ticket on Bambu’s support page with the Costco receipt and serial number, and ask what coverage applies.

Costco’s listing says one year, and Bambu’s 2-year US term is written for its own store. A written answer now beats an argument later. Save the reply with the receipt.

4Give the moving bed room

The A1’s bed slides front to back, so set it on a sturdy surface with clearance in front and behind.

A wobbly table shows up as ripples in prints. Our guide to 3D printer tables covers stands, load ratings and circuits.

5Update the firmware and bind the printer

Connect it to Bambu Handy or Bambu Studio and install the current firmware before the first real print.

Bambu sells region-specific printers and says one from the wrong region may not bind to an account or use cloud features. The Costco model number, PF002-A+SA005-US-COS, reads as a US unit; that’s our reading of the number, not Bambu’s.

6Run the calibrations and print one color first

Let the A1 run its full calibration, then print a single-color test before you load the AMS lite.

Bambu says the A1 calibrates its Z offset, bed level, vibration and nozzle pressure for every job. One clean single-color print tells you the printer is fine before color changes add variables.

7Load the AMS lite and keep the spares dry

Load the four spools, check that no PTFE tube is kinked, and seal up the spools you aren’t using.

The AMS lite is open to the room. Near the coast, marine-layer mornings mean damp air, and damp PLA strings and clogs. Keep spares in a sealed bin with desiccant.

8Label the spare hotends and learn the swap

Mark the 0.4 mm hardened steel and 0.2 mm stainless hotends and practice a swap while nothing is wrong.

Use the hardened steel hotend for carbon-fiber PLA or PETG and the 0.2 mm one for detail work in plain PLA or PETG. Put the stock hotend back for everyday printing.

Where Dreaming3D fits

We’re an independent repair shop in Carmel Valley, and where you bought the printer doesn’t matter to us. Here’s what we do for Costco buyers:

  • Setup: $159.99 per printer bought elsewhere, Costco included. We place it, calibrate it and run the first prints with you.
  • Repair: in person across San Diego County, $159.99 per printer, parts extra. Los Angeles by appointment; we confirm the date and price when you text.
  • Inside the warranty: we’ll ask you to open a Bambu ticket before we open the printer, and help you put together the photos, video and logs Bambu asks for.
  • Video help: live over Zoom or FaceTime, anywhere.
  • After Bambu’s warranty: our Lifetime Warranty plan is $24.99 a month for one printer, parts and labor, while the plan is active.
  • Printing instead: FDM at $7 a machine-hour and resin at $9, plus material, if you’d rather not own a printer at all.

What we don’t do: we don’t print metal, flight hardware, firearm components, load-bearing or safety-critical parts, or medical devices that touch patients.

A San Diego footnote: Costco’s own history says its first location opened in 1976, as Price Club, in a converted airplane hangar on Morena Boulevard. Bambu has no store of its own in San Diego that we know of (our Bambu retail post tracks where it’s opening), so for now a warehouse club is as close as Bambu retail gets here.

Common questions

Is the Costco Bambu Lab A1 Combo bundle a good deal?

It can be. On Nov 21 the bundle was $419.99, and the A1 Combo plus the same two hotends cost $382.98 on Bambu’s US store at its sale price. The four spools have to be worth $9.25 each to close the gap, which full 1 kg spools would be. If you only want the printer, Bambu’s store was cheaper. That’s our arithmetic on prices that change often.

What comes in the Costco Bambu Lab A1 Combo bundle?

Costco’s listing for item 2066547 lists the A1 printer with the AMS lite feeder, four PLA Basic spools, a 0.4 mm hardened steel hotend and a 0.2 mm stainless hotend. It doesn’t give the spools’ weight. A July version also included a $50 Bambu.com gift card; the Nov 21 box list didn’t.

Does a Costco A1 Combo get Bambu’s 2-year warranty?

Don’t count on it. Bambu’s policy page says the 2-year US and Canada extension applies to products bought through Bambu Store US and Bambu Store CA, and Costco’s listing says 1 year. Ask Bambu to confirm the coverage on your serial number with the Costco receipt.

Is Costco an authorized Bambu Lab reseller?

Costco wasn’t on Bambu’s US and Canada authorized reseller list when we checked on Nov 21. Bambu says only receipts from Bambu or distributors it authorizes are valid for warranty. The model number ends in -US-COS, which suggests a bundle packed for Costco, but that’s our inference. Ask Bambu before you rely on the warranty.

Can I return a 3D printer to Costco after 90 days?

Costco’s 90-day limit covers a named list of electronics, and 3D printers aren’t on it, so the general satisfaction guarantee appears to apply. The policy also says limitations apply. That’s our reading, not Costco’s answer, and we’re not lawyers. Ask at the membership counter and keep the box.

Is the Bambu Lab A1 enclosed?

No. Costco’s spec table says it is, but the A1 is an open-frame printer with a moving bed, and Bambu’s FAQ says it doesn’t recommend enclosing it. Bambu lists PLA, PETG, TPU and PVA as the A1’s ideal filaments.

Will Costco’s tech support help with a 3D printer?

Costco’s Technical and Warranty Services page lists free support for TVs, computers, tablets, cameras, appliances, home theater gear and printers, and doesn’t mention 3D printers. Call and ask, but expect to work through Bambu’s support or a local repair shop for A1 problems.

Will a local repair shop void my Bambu warranty?

It can, under Bambu’s terms. Its policy says the warranty becomes invalid if an unauthorized service center works on the printer without Bambu’s approval, and it asks owners to open a ticket before repairing anything. Inside the warranty, open the ticket first and get approval in writing. Outside it, any shop can work on it.

What isn’t covered by the warranty on an A1 Combo?

Bambu lists no warranty on the hotend and its parts, the extruder gears, build plates, PTFE tubes, the filament cutter, the nozzle wiper, and the AMS lite’s funnels and spool claws. The extruder unit and the AMS lite feeder unit get 3 months. Bambu says it may replace consumables that fail from a manufacturing defect while the printer is in warranty.

Do you fix Costco-bought Bambu printers in San Diego?

Yes, and where you bought it doesn’t matter. In-person repair across San Diego County is $159.99 per printer plus parts, setup for printers bought elsewhere is $159.99, Los Angeles is by appointment, and we help anywhere over Zoom or FaceTime. items.title: [justinangel.net] Windows Phone 7 – Emulator Automation
items.content_html:
Hi Folks,

In this next blog post we’ll review how to automate the Windows Phone 7 Emulator and what are some real-world usages this technique.

This blog post is the second blog post in a series of unrelated advanced Windows Phone 7 blog posts.
The previous blog post in this series is “Windows Phone 7 – Unlocked ROMs”.

 

Why is Windows Phone 7 Automation Important?

Currently, the Windows Phone 7 Emulator can only launch developer packages (XAPs) from inside Visual Studio 2010.
Meaning, if we’ve got a XAP we can’t get the emulator to load it without Visual Studio.

As we’ve seen in a previous blog post the emulator can be launched and even installed on machines that do not have Visual Studio. More on that here.
Let’s consider that in order to load XAPs into the Emulator we currently have to use Visual Studio. 

The problem is – How do we load XAPs into WP7 Emulators and Devices without using Visual Studio?

So how does our Build Server run nightly tests? Or how do our customers see our applications?

Customers and Build servers don't have Visual Studio 2010 installed.

So, how can we deploy XAPs to an emulator running on these machines?

 

Quit your Jibber-Jabber, show me how to automate the WP7 emulator!

Let’s create a new solution with a Console Application and a Windows Phone 7 Project.

We’ll use the ConsoleApplication as our automation harness that can run on any computer with the .Net framework.
The WindowsPhone Application is the application whose deployment we’ll automate.

 

The CoreCon 10 WP7 API

The secret sauce for WP7 Automation is the CoreCon API.
These CoreCon DLLs have been in deep hibernation since 2007 when they last got a major upgrade.
For WP7 Tools the CoreCon API has been updated and are used by Visual Studio 2010 when deploying applications to WP7 devices and emulators.

Let’s add a reference to Microsoft.SmartDevice.Connectivity.dll from the CoreCon API.
On a x64 developer box, the DLL can be found at: C:\Program Files (x86)\Common Files\microsoft shared\Phone Tools\CoreCon\10.0\Bin\Microsoft.Smartdevice.Connectivity.dll 

 

 

Now that we have the CoreCon DLL reference in place, we can start automating WP7.

Here’s the User Experience we’re aiming for in this demo:

We’ll have to build the following workflow:

     

We’ll start off by getting an instance of the WP7 CoreCon SDK instance to work with:

// Get CoreCon WP7 SDK

DatastoreManager dsmgrObj = new DatastoreManager(1033);

 

Platform WP7SDK = dsmgrObj.GetPlatforms().Single(p => p.Name == "New Windows Mobile 7 SDK");

 

Next up we’ll have to get a reference to either a WP7 physical device or a WP7 Emulator.
This demo will use the emulator, but if we set “useEmulator = false” this demo will try and connect to a physical WP7 device.

// Get Emulator / Device

bool useEmulator = true;

Device WP7Device = null;

if (useEmulator)

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Emulator");

else

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Device");

Now we’ll launch the WP7 Emulator/Device.
Note that the default WP7 Emulator Image is the one we’ll launch into, and in a previous blog post I’ve explained how to use the Unlocked ROM as the default ROM.

// Connect to WP7 Emulator / Device

Console.WriteLine("Connecting to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

WP7Device.Connect();

Console.WriteLine("Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device Connected...");

Next, we’ll have to check if our application is already installed, and if it is – we’ll uninstall it.
Since the the UpdateApplication Method in the current CoreCon API doesn’t work, this is our best bet on easily updating installed apps.

In order to Install or Uninstall our application, we’ll need it’s Application Product Identifier (GUID).
We can get the application GUID from the Properties/WMAppManifest.xml file.

 

We’ll write the code to check if an application is installed, and if it is – we’ll uninstall it.

Guid appID = new Guid("{5e75bba1-fbf6-463c-94ac-fa4a78f8fd12}");

RemoteApplication app;

if (WP7Device.IsApplicationInstalled(appID))

{

    Console.WriteLine("Uninstalling sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

    app = WP7Device.GetApplication(appID);

    app.Uninstall();

 

    Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP Uninstalled from Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

}

At this point, we’ll install our XAP.
In order to do that, we’ll need 3 pieces of information:
1. The location of our XAP.
2. The Application GUID.
3. The location of the application icon.

// Install XAP

Console.WriteLine("Installing sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

app = WP7Device.InstallApplication(

    appID,

    appID,

    "NormalApp",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\ApplicationIcon.png",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\Bin\Debug\WindowsPhoneApplication1.xap");

 

Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP installed to Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

The last step is to actually launch our application.

// Launch Application

Console.WriteLine("Launching sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

app.Launch();

Console.WriteLine("Launched sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

 

We’re done. And indeed when we run our sample application the app runs as expected:

 

So What is WP7 Automation good for?

There’s a lot of good use cases: Automating Unit tests, Loading Nightly builds into the emulator and even letting customers use the WP7 Emulator.
There’s really a plethora of reasons and situations WP7 Automation can prove useful in and it’s up to you to figure it out for your projects.

For instance in Vertigo, we’re using the WP7 Automation harness to run the WP7 Emulator on multi-touch laptops that our customers have.
So Vertigo’s customers, as part of an iterative process, get access to our current build without having to install or use Visual Studio 2010.

 

Access to Isolated Storage

One use-case in particular interests me, which is automating running all unit tests in the project after a Continuous Integration nightly build.

We can pretty much do all of the work to automate WP7 tests using WP7 Automation we’ve seen so far, but how do we get results into application? Or get instructions in?

The easiest method I can think off is communicate through cold storage – read & write files into Isolated Storage.

We’ll start off by writing a file into our WP7 Application IsoStore.
Remember that this code executes in the WP7 Emulator/Device.

public MainPage()

{

    InitializeComponent();

 

    SupportedOrientations = SupportedPageOrientation.Portrait | SupportedPageOrientation.Landscape;

 

    using (var isoStore = IsolatedStorageFile.GetUserStoreForApplication())

    using (var sw = new StreamWriter(isoStore.OpenFile("Foo.txt", FileMode.OpenOrCreate, FileAccess.Write)))

    {

        sw.Write("Hello WP7! (Written from WP7 IsoStore, read by Console Harness!)");

    }

}

Basically, We’ve written a Foo.txt file into our IsoStore and added some text into it.

Next, we would have used the RemoteIsolatedStorage class and get access to the emulator IsoStore, but that has not been enabled yet in CoreCon10.

We would have used RemoteApplication.GetIsolatedStorage() but that has not been implemented yet.

We’ll use a FileDeployer class instead.
There’s some reflection magic associated with getting a copy of a FileDeployer class that can be used for our application.

Thread.Sleep(10000);

//app.GetIsolatedStore(); <-- Throws NotImplementedException

object ConManServer = WP7Device.GetType().GetField("mConmanServer", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance).GetValue(WP7Device);

FileDeployer f = (FileDeployer)typeof(FileDeployer).GetConstructors(BindingFlags.Instance | BindingFlags.NonPublic)[0].Invoke(new object[] { ConManServer });

Next, we’ll copy the Foo.txt file from the application isolated storage into our local binary folder and read it into the console:

f.ReceiveFile(@"\Applications\Data\" + appID + @"\data\isolatedstore\Foo.txt", @"\Foo.txt");

 

Console.WriteLine("\t" + File.ReadAllText(@"foo.txt"));

 

When we run this sample we can see the text written from IsoStore showing up on our console.

And we’re done, we’ve esteblished a two-way communication channel between WP7 Emulator/Device and Managed .net code.  

 

Console WP7 Automation Harness Source Code

Here’s the source code we’ve built in this project:

// Get CoreCon WP7 SDK

DatastoreManager dsmgrObj = new DatastoreManager(1033);

 

Platform WP7SDK = dsmgrObj.GetPlatforms().Single(p => p.Name == "New Windows Mobile 7 SDK");

 

// Get Emulator / Device

bool useEmulator = true;

Device WP7Device = null;

if (useEmulator)

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Emulator");

else

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Device");

 

// Connect to WP7 Emulator / Device

Console.WriteLine("Connecting to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

WP7Device.Connect();

Console.WriteLine("Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device Connected...");

 

 

Guid appID = new Guid("{5e75bba1-fbf6-463c-94ac-fa4a78f8fd12}");

RemoteApplication app;

if (WP7Device.IsApplicationInstalled(appID))

{

    Console.WriteLine("Uninstalling sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

    app = WP7Device.GetApplication(appID);

    app.Uninstall();

 

    Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP Uninstalled from Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

}

 

// Install XAP

Console.WriteLine("Installing sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

app = WP7Device.InstallApplication(

    appID,

    appID,

    "NormalApp",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\ApplicationIcon.png",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\Bin\Debug\WindowsPhoneApplication1.xap");

 

Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP installed to Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

 

// Launch Application

Console.WriteLine("Launching sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

app.Launch();

Console.WriteLine("Launched sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

 

Console.WriteLine("Reading Foo.txt Isolated Storage file:");

 

Thread.Sleep(10000);

//app.GetIsolatedStore(); <-- Throws NotImplementedException

object ConManServer = WP7Device.GetType().GetField("mConmanServer", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance).GetValue(WP7Device);

FileDeployer f = (FileDeployer)typeof(FileDeployer).GetConstructors(BindingFlags.Instance | BindingFlags.NonPublic)[0].Invoke(new object[] { ConManServer });

f.ReceiveFile(@"\Applications\Data\" + appID + @"\data\isolatedstore\Foo.txt", @"\Foo.txt");

 

Console.WriteLine("\t" + File.ReadAllText(@"foo.txt"));

 

Console.ReadLine();

 

Fin

In this blog post we’ve talked about why Automating the WP7 Emulator and Device deployment process is important and how to go about doing that.
Hopefully now you know how to automate WP7 XAP Deployment.

In the next blog post in this series we’ll talk about setting up a Continuous Integration build for WP7.

 

Leave a Comment

Are there any other use cases for WP7 Automation?
Are you planning on using this technique somewhere?
Was this a good blog post? Sound off in the comments.

 

Sincerely,

-- Justin Angel

items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] #BehindThePrint 06: The Hidden Angle
items.content_html:
Behind the Scenes of Our Sandtable Creations

Through our Sandtable Exhibition projects, we explore the possibilities of 3D printing by creating detailed miniature worlds that bring together design, engineering, and craftsmanship.

In our #BehindThePrint series, we share the unexpected challenges, creative decisions, and practical lessons behind these creations.

Even the smallest architectural details in our miniature worlds can reveal unexpected 3D-printing challenges.

When the Corners Have Other Ideas

At first glance, there was nothing particularly unusual about the colorful geometric structures in our miniature climbing gym.

The raised details featured sloping edges designed at a 40° overhang angle. For our intended printing conditions, that seemed like a reasonable choice.

And for the most part, the prints looked fine.

Except for the corners.

While the straight edges appeared relatively clean, the corners developed rough, uneven surfaces. The problem was particularly noticeable around the green sections of the model.

The straight edges printed relatively cleanly, but the corners revealed unexpected surface defects

So what was different about those corners?

It looked like insufficient cooling was one factor affecting print quality. But the model’s geometry revealed another important part of the problem.

The corners weren’t actually following the same overhang angle as the edges.

And the difference was bigger than we might expect.

The Angle We Didn’t See

When designing an overhang, we usually pay attention to the angle of the sloping surface. If it falls within a range our printer can comfortably handle, the design should be reasonably printable.

Or so it seems.

The tricky part is that, on shapes with sharp corners, the angle we design along an edge isn’t necessarily the steepest angle the printer encounters.

Imagine a square column with a sloping section that gradually widens as it rises.

With every new layer, the edges extend slightly farther outward. Along a straight edge, this movement follows the intended 40° slope.

But something different happens at the corners.

Here, two edges meet, and their outward extensions combine diagonally. That means each corner reaches farther beyond the previous layer than the straight edges do.

Only a little farther, at first glance. But enough to change the effective overhang angle significantly.

The corner extends farther outward than the straight edge, creating a steeper effective overhang between successive layers.

For our four-sided shape, the numbers reveal just how much this matters.

The straight edges were designed at 40°.

At the corners, however, the effective overhang angle reached approximately 49.9°.

That’s almost 10° steeper than the original design angle!

For this production case, we were working with a maximum overhang target of 45°, allowing a margin for less favorable printing conditions.

The straight edges were within that target. The corners had quietly crossed it.

Suddenly, those rough corners made much more sense.

What Happens When We Change the Shape?

The interesting thing about this problem is that we don’t necessarily need to change the printer settings to address it.

Sometimes, we can make geometry work in our favor. And there are several ways to approach it.

More Sides, Less Trouble

What if our square shape wasn’t quite so square?

Imagine replacing the four-sided prism with one that has eight sides. The top-down shape becomes a little closer to a circle, and its corners become less pronounced.

That also changes how far those corners extend beyond the previous layer.

With the same 40° edge angle, the calculated maximum corner angle drops from approximately 49.9° to just 42.2°.

Adding more sides brings the effective corner overhang closer to the intended 40° edge angle.

The columns with multiple sides never faced the printing issues like the 4 sided version did

Of course, adding sides changes the appearance of the model. If a sharp, square shape is essential to the design, this might not be the ideal solution.

Fortunately, it isn’t the only option.

A Gentler Slope

Another approach is to keep the four-sided shape but reduce its straight edge angle.

For example, changing the edge angle from 40° to 35° reduces the calculated corner angle to approximately 44.7°.

That brings even the corners within our 45° design target.

It’s a relatively straightforward geometric adjustment, although the gentler slope also changes the proportions of the feature.

A gentler slope reduces the effective overhang angle at the corners without changing the number of sides.

Or Simply Soften the Corners

There’s also a third possibility: rounding the corners themselves.

Instead of allowing two straight edges to meet at a sharp point, we can introduce a curved transition.

This reduces the pronounced diagonal extension at the corner and can bring the maximum overhang closer to the intended edge angle.

Rounded corners reduce the abrupt change in geometry responsible for the steeper corner overhang.

Which approach makes the most sense depends on the design.

Sometimes we can change the overall shape. Other times, preserving its appearance matters more.

The important thing is understanding what the geometry is doing before deciding how to improve it.

By this point, you probably wonder about all these nice diagrams and calculations shared above. We have this handy little tool as a download link for you.

Feel free to check it out and explore how the straight slope or corner count will affect the corner angle.

A Different Way to Look at Overhangs

Our miniature climbing-gym component highlights a detail that’s surprisingly easy to overlook.

When we check an overhang, we’re often looking at the most obvious sloping surface. But the printer doesn’t only have to deal with that surface. It also has to build the corners where those surfaces meet.

And as we’ve seen, those corners can behave quite differently.

This doesn’t mean every sharp corner will cause printing problems. Actual print quality also depends on cooling, material, speed, and other conditions.

But it does give us another useful consideration when designing parts with overhangs: check the most demanding part of the geometry, not just the angle that’s easiest to see.

Sometimes, the trickiest overhang isn’t on the surface we’re looking at. It’s hiding right around the corner.

More Stories Behind the Print

From unexpected layer lines to hidden geometric challenges, our Sandtable projects keep reminding us that small design details can make a big difference.

Have you ever encountered a print that looked perfectly reasonable in the model but turned out differently than expected?

We’d love to hear what you discovered.

See you in the next #BehindThePrint!

items.title: [homekits.de] IKEA lists Liljebagge radiator thermostat for €14.99 in Germany
items.content_html: IKEA has listed the Liljebagge radiator thermostat for €14.99 in its German online store, but it cannot be ordered there yet. According to HomeKits, sales are scheduled to begin in January 2027. Sales could begin earlier at some individual stores. The device is designed for water-based radiators and communicates via Matter over Thread. Integration requires a Thread border router, but not necessarily the IKEA Dirigera hub; the temperature can also be set directly on the thermostat. However, initial customer reviews from Sweden mention discrepancies in temperature readings and bothersome noises during adjustment.
